catalog_quote: II. Accentuation. 1° Dans chaque mot pounou, il y a au moins une syllabe accentuée. Cet accent consiste en une élévation de la tonalité et un appui de la voix sur la ou les syllabes accentuées. 2° L'accent se place sur la syllabe racine, c'est-à-dire, sur la pénultième, pour les mots simples. Exemples : Rŭ-ga, viens; du-săl-a, plume. Remarque. — Il faut excepter les noms à racine incomplète, selon le schéma C.V. où l'accent se place sur le préfixe nominal. Exemples : Bŭ-ta, fusil; dĭ-tu, sangsue. 3° Dans les mots à suffixes, l'accent se place aussi sur la syllabe racine Ces suffixes sont les suivants : ila, ulu, una, unu, ena. Exemples : Rŭg-ila, viens pour; i-tsăn-unu, siège; u-kŏb-ena, être emmêlé. Remarque. — Les verbes dérivés en anga, ungu, esena, usunu ont l'accent sur la pénultième, selon ă-nga, ŭ-ngu. Exemple : Rug-ă-nga, viens souvent. 4° Dans les verbes de quatre syllabes,…

new_statements.translation: 1. In every Punu word there is at least one accented syllable. This accent consists of a raising of pitch and a reinforcement of the voice on the accented syllable(s). 2. The accent falls on the root syllable, i.e. on the penultimate, for simple words. Examples: Rùg-a 'come', du-sǎl-a 'feather'. Remark: nouns with an incomplete (C-V) root are excepted; there the accent falls on the noun prefix (Bù-ta 'gun', dì-tu 'leech'). 3. In suffixed words the accent also falls on the root syllable [...] (Rǔg-ila 'come for', i-tsǎn-unu 'seat') [...] Remark: derived verbs in -anga, -ungu, -esena, -usunu have the accent on the penultimate.
new_statements.citation: Bonneau, Joseph (R. P.). 1940. Grammaire pounou. Journal de la Société des Africanistes 10: 131-161 (DOI 10.3406/jafr.1940.2490).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: VERBATIM CHECK. Opened (lines 112-123, Persée page 136) and the page image. Section 'II. Accentuation' is there at p.136 exactly as located, points 1°-4°. The quoted French matches the printed page word for word except for the transcription of the examples: the page prints 'Rŭ-ga, viens; du-săl-a, plume' (reporter: 'Rùg-a... du-sǎl-a'), 'Bŭ-ta, fusil; dĭ-tu, sangsue' (reporter: 'Bù-ta... dì-tu'), 'Rŭg-ila... i-tsăn-unu... u-kŏb-ena', 'selon ă-nga, ŭ-ngu', 'Rug-ă-nga', 'Rŭg-il-ă-nga' — Bonneau marks the accented vowel with a breve/hacek-like diacritic, not grave; segmentation of the first example is Rŭ-ga not Rùg-a. Wording of the rule sentences (1° 'Dans chaque mot pounou, il y a au moins u…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (described as combined pitch raising and intensity) falls on the root (stem-initial) syllable, which is the penult in unsuffixed disyllabic-stem words; it stays on the root syllable when applicative/other suffixes are added, except that verbs with the extensions -anga/-ungu/-esena/-usunu accent the penult; nouns with monosyllabic C-V roots accent the class prefix.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.136 point 4°: in four-syllable verbs with penult accent a lighter accent falls on the first syllable (Rùg-il-ǎ-nga 'come often for').
new_statements.exceptions: C-V-root nouns accent the prefix (Bú-ta, dí-tu); derived verbs in -anga, -ungu, -esena, -usunu have penultimate rather than root accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms; 1940 missionary description that explicitly merges pitch ('élévation de la tonalité') and force. All later work (Nsuka-Nkutsi ed. 1980; Blanchon 1988-1999; Yukawa 2005; Tomba Moussavou 2007) analyses Punu as a tone language (H/L plus supra-high, 'tone cases'), and Hyman 2006/2009 report stem-initial positional privileges (mid vowels and vowel length only in the first root syllable), so Bonneau's 'accent' most likely reflects H tone plus stem-initial prominence rather than an independent stress system. Variety: forest groups of Moukaba, Mwabi, Yanga etc. (south Gabon).
new_statements.identity_note: Bonneau describes the Punu ('pounou') of the forest groups between the Nyanga and Ngounié (Moukaba, Mwabi, Yanga etc., south Gabon) = punu1239; Yukawa's 2005 speaker is from Tchibanga (Gabon). No separate dialect glottocode involved.

sources.note: p.136 'II. Accentuation': every word has at least one accented syllable (pitch rise + force); accent on the root syllable = penult in simple words (Rùg-a, du-sǎl-a); C-V-root nouns accent the prefix (Bú-ta, dí-tu); suffixed words keep accent on root syllable (Rúg-ila, i-tsǎn-unu); derived verbs in -anga/-ungu/-esena/-usunu accent the penult (Rug-ǎ-nga); 4-syllable verbs with penult accent get a lighter accent on the first syllable (Rùg-il-ǎ-nga).

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2006. Word-prosodic typology. Phonology 23: 225-257; Hyman 2009 (UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report) on penultimate/positional length in Bantu.
sources.note: Second-hand: Punu restricts mid vowels /ɛ ɔ/ to the first root syllable (citing Fontaney 1980, Kwenzi Mikala 1980) and vowel length to a stem-initial penult (Blanchon database) — positional prominence of stem-initial syllable, discussed as culminative but not called stress.
